label: Defect level and the Williams-Brown model
prereqs: Wafer probe, final test and burn-in
lesson:
# Defect level and the Williams-Brown model

Customers buy quality, not coverage. The defect level, the fraction of shipped parts that are defective, is usually quoted in defective parts per million (DPPM), and it depends on two quantities a test engineer knows: process yield and fault coverage. The Williams-Brown model links them and turns a DPPM target into a coverage target, which is how coverage sign-off thresholds are justified.

## The model

Let $Y$ be the yield (fraction of good dies) and $T$ the fault coverage of the test. Williams and Brown modeled faults as independent and equally likely, so a die is good with probability $Y$ and a die passes the test if none of its faults is in the detected fraction. The probability that a passing part is defective is
$$DL = 1 - Y^{1 - T}.$$
At $T = 1$, $DL = 0$; at $T = 0$, $DL = 1 - Y$, the fraction of all dies that are bad. For $Y = 0.4$ and $T = 0.9324$, $DL = 1 - 0.4^{0.0676} = 0.0601$, about 60,000 DPPM: even 93 percent coverage ships many bad parts when yield is low.

## Coverage for a target

Inverting the model gives the coverage needed for a quality goal:
$$T = 1 - \frac{\ln(1 - DL)}{\ln Y}.$$
For $Y = 0.95$ and 500 DPPM, $T = 1 - \ln(0.9995)/\ln(0.95) = 99.025$ percent. Lower yield demands higher coverage for the same DPPM, which is why new processes, with low yield, are the hardest to ship at quality. Automotive targets near single-digit DPPM push coverage requirements toward the limit of the stuck-at model and motivate additional fault models.

## Connecting to defect density

With Poisson random defects, $Y = e^{-AD_0}$ for die area $A$ and defect density $D_0$, and then $Y^{1-T} = e^{-AD_0(1-T)}$: only the untested fraction of the defects reaches the customer. A 56 mm$^2$ die at 0.37 defects per cm$^2$ has $Y = 0.813$; at 97.94 percent coverage, $DL \approx 4260$ DPPM. The model assumes fault coverage measures defect coverage, which overstates quality when real defects behave unlike modeled faults; refinements weight faults by their likelihood or use multiple-detect coverage.

## Going deeper

Williams and Brown, "Defect level as a function of fault coverage," IEEE Transactions on Computers, 1981; Bushnell and Agrawal (2000), chapter 3.

problems.q: A process yields 70 percent good dies and the test set has 95.99 percent fault coverage. Using the Williams-Brown model, what is the defect level of shipped parts, in defective parts per million? Round to the nearest integer.

A process yields 86 percent good dies and the test set has 95.62 percent fault coverage. Using the Williams-Brown model, what is the defect level of shipped parts, in defective parts per million? Round to the nearest integer.

A process yields 80 percent good dies and the test set has 91.37 percent fault coverage. Using the Williams-Brown model, what is the defect level of shipped parts, in defective parts per million? Round to the nearest integer.

A product's yield is 64 percent and the customer requires at most 1000 defective parts per million. Using the Williams-Brown model, what fault coverage is needed, in percent? Round to 3 decimal places.

A product's yield is 87 percent and the customer requires at most 100 defective parts per million. Using the Williams-Brown model, what fault coverage is needed, in percent? Round to 3 decimal places.

A product's yield is 66 percent and the customer requires at most 1000 defective parts per million. Using the Williams-Brown model, what fault coverage is needed, in percent? Round to 3 decimal places.

A 590 mm$^2$ die is built in a process with 0.26 random killer defects per cm$^2$ (Poisson yield) and tested to 99.56 percent fault coverage. Using Williams-Brown, what is the defect level, in DPPM? Round to the nearest integer.
problems.e: $Y = e^{-1.534} = 0.2157$; $DL = 1 - Y^{0.0044} = 6727$ DPPM. Since $Y^{1-T} = e^{-AD_0(1-T)}$, only the untested fraction of defects reaches the customer.

problems.q: A 65 mm$^2$ die is built in a process with 0.06 random killer defects per cm$^2$ (Poisson yield) and tested to 97.32 percent fault coverage. Using Williams-Brown, what is the defect level, in DPPM? Round to the nearest integer.

label: Fault diagnosis and yield learning
prereqs: Serial fault simulation and fault dropping
Defect level and the Williams-Brown model
lesson:
# Fault diagnosis and yield learning

When a die fails, the tester log says which patterns failed at which outputs. Diagnosis turns that log into candidate defect locations, and volume diagnosis across thousands of failing dies turns those candidates into the yield-learning signal that tells the fab which layer and mechanism to fix. It is the test flow's feedback loop to manufacturing, and an inference problem a tool designer can attack with dictionaries, cone analysis and statistics.

## Dictionary matching

**Cause-effect** diagnosis simulates candidate faults and compares their predicted behaviour with the observed one. A **pass/fail dictionary** stores, for each fault, the set of patterns it fails. Score each candidate by the mismatch between prediction and observation, the size of the symmetric difference of the two pattern sets. If a die fails patterns {P3, P4, P5, P6, P9} and candidates predict {P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P7, P9}, {P3, P4, P5, P6, P9} and {P3, P5, P6, P7, P9}, their scores are 4, 0 and 2, and the second matches perfectly. A full-response dictionary also records which outputs fail, which resolves more candidates at a cost of $F \times P \times O$ bits instead of $F \times P$; production tools simulate candidates on demand instead of storing dictionaries.

## Effect-cause analysis

**Effect-cause** diagnosis reasons backward from the failures. Under a single-fault assumption, the defect must lie in the fan-in cone of every failing output on a failing pattern, so intersecting those cones bounds the candidates. Outputs that passed cannot simply be subtracted, because a fault in their cone need not reach them on that pattern. Intersections over many patterns, followed by simulation of the survivors, typically localize a defect to a few nets, which layout then maps to physical locations for failure analysis. Multiple defects, bridges and cell-internal faults require scoring methods that tolerate partial matches.

## Yield learning

**Volume diagnosis** aggregates candidates over many failing dies, attributes them to layers and mechanisms using layout (a candidate net that runs mostly on metal 2 next to a neighbour suggests a metal-2 short), and builds a Pareto of yield loss. With Poisson yield and mechanism contributions $\lambda_i$ to the expected killer defects per die, removing mechanism $j$ raises yield from $e^{-\sum \lambda_i}$ to $e^{-(\sum \lambda_i - \lambda_j)}$. If poly shorts contribute 0.26 of a total 0.53, eliminating them raises yield from 58.9 to 76.3 percent, which tells the fab where its effort pays most.

## Going deeper

Abramovici, Breuer and Friedman (1990), chapter 12; Wang, Wu and Wen (2006), chapter 7; Tang et al. and other volume-diagnosis papers at the International Test Conference.

problems.q: A failing die fails patterns {P4, P5, P6, P8} out of P1 to P8. A pass/fail fault dictionary lists the failing patterns each candidate fault predicts: C1 predicts {P4, P5, P6}; C2 predicts {P5, P8}; C3 predicts {P4, P5, P6, P8}. Scoring each candidate by the number of patterns where prediction and observation disagree, which candidate number matches best?
problems.e: Mismatch counts (size of the symmetric difference): C1: 1, C2: 2, C3: 0.

problems.q: A failing die fails patterns {P2, P5, P6} out of P1 to P12. A pass/fail fault dictionary lists the failing patterns each candidate fault predicts: C1 predicts {P2, P5, P10}; C2 predicts {P2, P5, P6, P8}; C3 predicts {P2, P6, P12}. Scoring each candidate by the number of patterns where prediction and observation disagree, which candidate number matches best?
problems.e: Mismatch counts (size of the symmetric difference): C1: 2, C2: 1, C3: 2.

problems.q: A failing die fails patterns {P2, P5, P8} out of P1 to P11. A pass/fail fault dictionary lists the failing patterns each candidate fault predicts: C1 predicts {P2, P5, P8, P9}; C2 predicts {P2, P5, P6}; C3 predicts {P2, P4, P5, P6, P8}. Scoring each candidate by the number of patterns where prediction and observation disagree, which candidate number matches best?
problems.e: Mismatch counts (size of the symmetric difference): C1: 1, C2: 2, C3: 2.

problems.q: Inputs a, b, c, d; g1 = AND(a, d); g2 = OR(b, g1); g3 = NAND(c, g2); g4 = NAND(a, d); g5 = OR(g1, g3); g6 = NOR(c, g5); primary outputs g4 and g6. On one pattern the tester sees wrong values on g4 only. Under the single-fault assumption, the defect lies on a stem in the fan-in cone of every failing output. How many stems (inputs and gate outputs) are candidates?
problems.e: Intersecting the fan-in cones leaves a, d, g4: 3 candidates. Passing outputs cannot simply be subtracted, because a fault in their cone need not reach them on this pattern.

problems.q: Inputs a, b, c, d; g1 = NOR(b, c); g2 = AND(c, d); g3 = OR(d, g1); g4 = NOR(a, g3); g5 = OR(d, g4); g6 = OR(b, g2); primary outputs g5 and g6. On one pattern the tester sees wrong values on g5 only. Under the single-fault assumption, the defect lies on a stem in the fan-in cone of every failing output. How many stems (inputs and gate outputs) are candidates?
problems.e: Intersecting the fan-in cones leaves a, b, c, d, g1, g3, g4, g5: 8 candidates. Passing outputs cannot simply be subtracted, because a fault in their cone need not reach them on this pattern.

problems.q: Inputs a, b, c, d; g1 = NAND(c, d); g2 = AND(a, g1); g3 = NOR(a, g2); g4 = OR(a, b); g5 = NOR(d, g3); g6 = OR(a, g1); g7 = AND(g5, g6); primary outputs g4 and g7. On one pattern the tester sees wrong values on g4 and g7 only. Under the single-fault assumption, the defect lies on a stem in the fan-in cone of every failing output. How many stems (inputs and gate outputs) are candidates?
problems.e: Intersecting the fan-in cones leaves a: 1 candidates. Passing outputs cannot simply be subtracted, because a fault in their cone need not reach them on this pattern.

problems.q: Volume diagnosis and failure analysis attribute the expected number of killer defects per die to mechanisms: via opens 0.02, metal-2 shorts 0.26, metal-1 shorts 0.22, poly shorts 0.29. With Poisson yield, what would the yield become if the largest mechanism were eliminated, in percent? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Today $Y = e^{-0.79} = 45.38$ percent. Removing poly shorts leaves $\lambda = 0.5$, so $Y = 60.65$ percent. Ranking mechanisms this way is the Pareto step of yield learning.

problems.q: Volume diagnosis and failure analysis attribute the expected number of killer defects per die to mechanisms: via opens 0.12, metal-2 shorts 0.27, metal-1 shorts 0.03. With Poisson yield, what would the yield become if the largest mechanism were eliminated, in percent? Round to 2 decimal places.

With Poisson yield, what would the yield become if the largest mechanism were eliminated, in percent? Round to 2 decimal places.

label: Silicon debug and post-silicon validation
lesson:
# Silicon debug and post-silicon validation

First silicon runs real software at full speed, billions of cycles per second, and finds bugs that pre-silicon simulation never reached. Post-silicon validation hunts those design and electrical bugs; silicon debug localizes them with very little visibility into the chip. Its tools, trace buffers, triggers, scan dumps and JTAG-based access, are design-for-debug structures that reuse much of the test infrastructure.

## Validation versus manufacturing test

Manufacturing test assumes the design is correct and screens each die for defects; its patterns are structural and its question is whether this die was built right. **Post-silicon validation** assumes the dies are mostly good and asks whether the design works: it runs operating systems, stress tests and random instruction streams across voltage, temperature and frequency. Failures that appear on every die point to design bugs; failures that depend on conditions, mapped with **shmoo plots** of pass and fail over voltage and frequency, point to speed paths, noise or power integrity. A validation escape is a bug in every part; a test escape is a defective part that passed test.

## Seeing inside: traces and triggers

The central difficulty is **observability**: a few internal signals can be watched while the chip runs at speed. An on-chip **trace buffer** records selected signals each cycle after a programmable **trigger** fires on a condition such as a bus value. Its capacity limits the window. With 1024 entries of 32 bits and 24 traced signals, each cycle's sample fits in one entry and 1024 cycles are captured; tracing 70 signals in 32-bit entries needs 3 entries per cycle and captures only 341. **Trace signal selection** chooses signals from which many untraced flop values can be reconstructed, and compression widens the window further.

## Scan dumps and reproduction

A **scan dump** stops the functional clocks at a trigger and shifts out all scan chains, giving the complete state at one instant at the cost of destroying execution. Combining dumps at successive stop points with traces localizes the failing window; then the window is reproduced in simulation or emulation, where visibility is complete, to find the root cause. Non-determinism from asynchronous clock crossings can stop a failure from reproducing, so debug flows include deterministic modes. Fixes use spare cells and metal-only ECOs or microcode and firmware patches when they exist, avoiding a full respin.

## Going deeper

Mishra, Morad, Ludwig and others, "Post-Silicon Validation and Debug" (2019); Abramovici et al., "A reconfigurable design-for-debug infrastructure for SoCs," Design Automation Conference, 2006.

problems.q:
A bug appears only after billions of cycles of an operating system boot on real silicon. Why was it not found in pre-silicon simulation?

A) Pre-silicon verification never runs software

B) Simulation runs many orders of magnitude slower, so such long scenarios were never executed

C) Simulation cannot model processors

D) The bug is always a manufacturing defect
problems.a: Simulation runs many orders of magnitude slower, so such long scenarios were never executed
problems.e: Silicon runs at full speed and reaches deep states; that speed is why validation finds bugs simulation missed, and why it observes so little.

problems.q:
A trigger unit compares bus values every cycle and fires when a pattern appears. Why is it essential?

A) It increases the clock frequency

B) It replaces the trace buffer

C) Trace and scan capture are limited in size, so they must start or stop near the event of interest

D) It runs ATPG on chip
problems.a: Trace and scan capture are limited in size, so they must start or stop near the event of interest
problems.e: A small window of observation is only useful if it is placed around the failure; programmable triggers place it.

problems.q:
A bug appears only after billions of cycles of an operating system boot on real silicon. Why was it not found in pre-silicon simulation?

A) Simulation runs many orders of magnitude slower, so such long scenarios were never executed

B) Pre-silicon verification never runs software

C) The bug is always a manufacturing defect

D) Simulation cannot model processors
problems.a: Simulation runs many orders of magnitude slower, so such long scenarios were never executed
problems.e: Silicon runs at full speed and reaches deep states; that speed is why validation finds bugs simulation missed, and why it observes so little.

problems.q:
An on-chip trace buffer has 512 entries of 128 bits. The debug engineer traces 203 signals every cycle, and each cycle's sample occupies $\lceil 203/128 \rceil$ consecutive entries. After the trigger, how many consecutive cycles can be captured before the buffer is full?

A) 256

B) 170

C) 512

D) 322
problems.e: Each sample takes 2 of the 128-bit entries, so 512/2 = 256 cycles fit. Tracing fewer signals or compressing them widens the window.

problems.q:
An on-chip trace buffer has 2048 entries of 128 bits. The debug engineer traces 258 signals every cycle, and each cycle's sample occupies $\lceil 258/128 \rceil$ consecutive entries. After the trigger, how many consecutive cycles can be captured before the buffer is full?

A) 512

B) 2048

C) 682

D) 1016
problems.e: Each sample takes 3 of the 128-bit entries, so 2048/3 = 682 cycles fit. Tracing fewer signals or compressing them widens the window.

problems.q:
An on-chip trace buffer has 2048 entries of 32 bits. The debug engineer traces 66 signals every cycle, and each cycle's sample occupies $\lceil 66/32 \rceil$ consecutive entries. After the trigger, how many consecutive cycles can be captured before the buffer is full?

A) 992

B) 512

C) 682

D) 2048
problems.e: Each sample takes 3 of the 32-bit entries, so 2048/3 = 682 cycles fit. Tracing fewer signals or compressing them widens the window.

problems.q:
Why do debug architectures often reuse the JTAG TAP?

A) IEEE 1149.1 requires debug features

B) It is already present, standard and reachable on the board, so debug registers can be accessed without new pins

C) Debug logic must be on the boundary register

D) JTAG is faster than any functional interface
problems.a: It is already present, standard and reachable on the board, so debug registers can be accessed without new pins
problems.e: The TAP is the universal low-pin-count access port; debug and IJTAG instruments ride on it.

problems.q:
Why is non-determinism a major obstacle in silicon debug of multi-clock systems?

A) Scan chains randomize their contents

B) Trace buffers lose data

C) Triggers fire randomly

D) Asynchronous clock domains make the same test take different cycle-level paths, so a failure may not reproduce
problems.a: Asynchronous clock domains make the same test take different cycle-level paths, so a failure may not reproduce
problems.e: Crossing timing varies run to run; debug flows force deterministic modes or record enough to replay.

problems.q:
What is trace signal selection trying to maximize?

A) The number of signals per entry regardless of content

B) The trace buffer depth

C) The number of untraced internal states that can be reconstructed from the traced signals

D) The fault coverage
problems.a: The number of untraced internal states that can be reconstructed from the traced signals
problems.e: With restoration, traced flops let tools infer neighbours' values; good selection maximizes that restoration ratio.

label: ATPG as a callable skill
prereqs: Engines as agent tools over MCP
lesson:
# ATPG as a callable skill

In an agent-first flow, ATPG is not a program an engineer babysits but a skill that agents select and call: a compiled engine with golden tests and a manifest that states what it does, what it takes, what it returns and what may be tuned. Designing that skill well means deciding which parts of the ATPG engine are immutable core, which are policy and parameters, and which typed results downstream agents need.

## The manifest and the typed interface

An agent chooses a skill by reading manifests, not source. An ATPG manifest states the supported fault models (stuck-at, transition, cell-aware), required inputs (netlist, scan and clock definitions, fault list, constraints), outputs (patterns in STIL, a coverage report broken down by fault class, pattern count and shift length) and the tunable knobs (abort limit, compaction effort, fault ordering, X handling). Exposed as a tool with typed inputs and outputs, for example over MCP, the skill lets a test-time agent compute cost as patterns times shift cycles without parsing logs, and lets a planner choose between a fast structural engine and a SAT-based engine by their advertised strengths: the SAT engine for many aborted or suspected redundant faults.

## Core, policy and parameters

The **immutable core** is what coverage numbers rest on: fault simulation must never report a pattern as detecting a fault it does not detect, and five-valued evaluation and implication must be correct. **Policy** is how the search proceeds: fault ordering, backtrace heuristics, dynamic compaction strategy, and fault models plugged in at a defined extension point. **Parameters** are the backtrack limit, effort levels and pattern caps. A request for fewer patterns at the same coverage lands at Tier 1 (raise compaction effort, change ordering parameters); a new defect model from a cell-aware table lands at Tier 2 (a plug-in fault model); a change to the implication engine is Tier 3 and needs human review and full regression.

## Safety and reward

An ATPG skill sees the customer's netlist, so it runs sandboxed with no network: the IP boundary is part of the architecture. It must be deterministic and seedable, so a result can be compared with a baseline and attributed to a change. If agents are rewarded on coverage, they can learn to game it: test coverage rises when more faults are declared untestable, so the reward must check that untestable classifications are proven, that the fault list is unchanged, and that pattern count is held within bounds.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum (skills, manifests, change tiers); the Fault open-source ATPG and the OpenROAD flow for examples of scriptable DFT engines.

problems.q:
Why should an agent call the compiled ATPG engine instead of writing its own test generator for each request?

A) Agents cannot generate any code

B) ATPG engines have no parameters

C) The engine is always slower than generated code

D) The engine is fast, verified and deterministic; the agent's job is selection and configuration, not re-implementing search
problems.a: The engine is fast, verified and deterministic; the agent's job is selection and configuration, not re-implementing search
problems.e: Selection is a cheap text decision; the expensive, correctness-critical compute stays in the engine.

problems.q:
An ATPG skill is exposed as a typed tool to other agents. Which output field matters most for a downstream test-time agent?

A) The pattern count and per-pattern shift length, alongside the coverage achieved

B) The ATPG run's log verbosity

C) The source file names of the engine

D) The license server address
problems.a: The pattern count and per-pattern shift length, alongside the coverage achieved
problems.e: Test time is pattern count times shift cycles; a typed result lets the next agent compute cost without parsing logs.

problems.q:
Why should an agent call the compiled ATPG engine instead of writing its own test generator for each request?

A) The engine is fast, verified and deterministic; the agent's job is selection and configuration, not re-implementing search

B) ATPG engines have no parameters

C) Agents cannot generate any code

D) The engine is always slower than generated code
problems.a: The engine is fast, verified and deterministic; the agent's job is selection and configuration, not re-implementing search
problems.e: Selection is a cheap text decision; the expensive, correctness-critical compute stays in the engine.

problems.q:
A customer asks for fewer patterns at the same coverage. Which change tier should the agent try first?

A) Tier 2: add a new fault model

B) Tier 3: rewrite PODEM's backtrace

C) Tier 3: change the fault simulator's value system

D) Tier 1: raise the compaction effort and adjust the fault ordering parameters
problems.a: Tier 1: raise the compaction effort and adjust the fault ordering parameters
problems.e: Pattern count responds to existing configuration knobs; the smallest safe tier is configuration.

problems.q:
A customer asks for fewer patterns at the same coverage. Which change tier should the agent try first?

A) Tier 3: rewrite PODEM's backtrace

B) Tier 2: add a new fault model

C) Tier 1: raise the compaction effort and adjust the fault ordering parameters

D) Tier 3: change the fault simulator's value system
problems.a: Tier 1: raise the compaction effort and adjust the fault ordering parameters
problems.e: Pattern count responds to existing configuration knobs; the smallest safe tier is configuration.

problems.q:
A team wants ATPG to target a new defect type described by a cell-aware table. Which tier does this land in?

A) Tier 2: a plug-in fault model at the engine's fault-model extension point

B) Tier 3: a change to the D-calculus

C) Tier 1: a single parameter

D) No change: stuck-at already covers it
problems.a: Tier 2: a plug-in fault model at the engine's fault-model extension point
problems.e: A new fault model is a defined extension (activation and propagation conditions) without touching the search core.

problems.q:
An agent's reward for an ATPG experiment is coverage alone. What can it learn to game?

A) Declaring hard faults untestable or excluding them, which raises test coverage without better tests

B) Making the netlist larger

C) Running ATPG twice

D) Nothing: coverage cannot be gamed
problems.a: Declaring hard faults untestable or excluding them, which raises test coverage without better tests
problems.e: A reward must check that untestable classifications are proven and that pattern count and fault lists stay comparable.

problems.q:
An ATPG tool skill runs in a sandbox with no network. Why?

A) Design netlists are the customer's IP; the skill must not be able to send them anywhere

B) Network access slows ATPG

C) ATPG needs a GPU

D) Sandboxes improve coverage
problems.a: Design netlists are the customer's IP; the skill must not be able to send them anywhere
problems.e: The IP boundary is architectural: skills see design data, so they must not have an exfiltration path.

problems.q:
An agent must choose between a fast structural ATPG skill and a SAT-based one for a block with many aborted faults. What should drive the choice?

A) Always both, on every fault

B) Always the structural one, because it is first in the list

C) Whichever has the shorter manifest

D) The manifests' stated strengths: SAT-based ATPG resolves hard and redundant faults that structural search aborts
problems.a: The manifests' stated strengths: SAT-based ATPG resolves hard and redundant faults that structural search aborts
problems.e: Skill selection matches the situation (many aborts) to the capability advertised (proving or finding hard faults).

label: Agents that insert and verify test logic
lesson:
# Agents that insert and verify test logic

DFT insertion, scan stitching, compression, test points and wrappers, is a natural target for agents: it is configuration-driven, it has clear rules, and it has strong automatic checks. The agent's job is not to edit netlists freely but to propose configurations, run the insertion engine, and prove with equivalence, design-rule and coverage checks that the change did what was intended and nothing else.

## What the agent must prove

Every insertion is checked three ways. **Function**: with scan enable and test modes tied to functional values, the scan muxes and test points are transparent, so combinational equivalence checking (a miter between pre- and post-insertion netlists) must prove the two equivalent. **Structure**: scan design rules (controllable clocks and resets, no loops) must pass, and a **chain integrity** test that shifts a known pattern such as 0011 through every chain must come out intact, because equivalence in functional mode says nothing about the scan path. **Testability**: ATPG coverage and pattern count must meet or beat the baseline.

## The harness loop

The agent works in the edit-build-test loop. It proposes a configuration (chain count, compression ratio, test-point budget, ordering policy), the harness runs insertion, DRC, equivalence and ATPG, and compares coverage and pattern counts with the golden baseline. Failures go back to the agent as feedback; success produces a reviewable diff with the evidence attached for a human. Most requests land at Tier 1 (configuration) or Tier 2 (a plug-in selection rule, such as placing test points only in modules that miss coverage); the netlist database and insertion mechanics are core and are not edited.

## Invariants versus proxies

Proxies invite trade-offs against invariants. An agent rewarded for balanced chains may cross clock domains without lockup latches and create hold failures in shift; one rewarded for fewer test points may raise pattern count. A coverage drop after a passing equivalence check is a regression, typically from new tied or blocked logic, and must be diagnosed before promotion. Configurations must be versioned and replayable on the next netlist. When a recipe works, the skill flywheel promotes the recipe and the knowledge of when to use it into the shared library; the customer's netlist stays on site.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum (harness loop, golden testing, skill flywheel); Wang, Wu and Wen (2006), chapter 2, for scan design rules.

problems.q:
An agent inserts scan into a netlist. Which check proves it did not change the design's function?

A) Combinational equivalence checking between the pre- and post-insertion netlists with scan enable tied to functional mode

B) Comparing file sizes

C) Running ATPG and looking at coverage

D) Static timing analysis alone
problems.a: Combinational equivalence checking between the pre- and post-insertion netlists with scan enable tied to functional mode
problems.e: With scan enable at 0 the scan muxes are transparent, so the two netlists must be equivalent; a miter-based checker proves it.

problems.q:
After an agent stitches scan chains, which test catches a chain broken by a wrong connection?

A) Equivalence checking in functional mode

B) A chain integrity (flush) test that shifts a known pattern such as 0011 through each chain and checks it arrives intact

C) A stuck-at ATPG run only

D) A March test
problems.a: A chain integrity (flush) test that shifts a known pattern such as 0011 through each chain and checks it arrives intact
problems.e: Functional equivalence ignores the scan path; only shifting through the chain proves its continuity and length.

problems.q:
Which scan design-rule violation must an insertion agent fix before ATPG can use a flop?

A) A flop whose clock or asynchronous reset is not controllable from the test clocks and pins

B) A flop on a timing-critical path

C) A flop with a long name

D) A flop with high fanout
problems.a: A flop whose clock or asynchronous reset is not controllable from the test clocks and pins
problems.e: Uncontrollable clocks or resets make scan shifting unpredictable, so the flop cannot be part of a chain until fixed.

problems.q:
An insertion agent proposes adding an observation point on a high-fanout net. What must it re-verify?

A) Only the chain length

B) Functional equivalence (the point must be transparent in functional mode), timing on that net, and the coverage gain

C) Nothing: observation points are passive

D) Only the coverage gain
problems.a: Functional equivalence (the point must be transparent in functional mode), timing on that net, and the coverage gain
problems.e: A test point adds load and logic; it must not change function, must not break timing, and must actually help coverage.

problems.q:
A customer wants test points inserted only in modules that miss coverage. Which tier?

A) No tier: test points cannot be targeted

B) Tier 1 or 2: configuration of the test-point policy, or a plug-in selection rule

C) Tier 3: rewrite the netlist database

D) Tier 3: change the fault simulator
problems.a: Tier 1 or 2: configuration of the test-point policy, or a plug-in selection rule
problems.e: Where to place test points is policy; the insertion mechanics and netlist database are core and need not change.

problems.q:
Why should the agent's scan insertion be reproducible from a configuration file?

A) So the change is versioned, reviewable and reversible, and can be replayed on the next netlist

B) Configuration files are faster to read

C) Reproducibility lowers test coverage

D) Netlists cannot be versioned
problems.a: So the change is versioned, reviewable and reversible, and can be replayed on the next netlist
problems.e: Every engine change must be versioned and reversible; a configuration-driven insertion is an auditable artifact.

problems.q:
An agent inserts scan and all checks pass, but test coverage dropped 0.5 points versus baseline. What is the right action?

A) Lower the baseline

B) Promote it, since equivalence passed

C) Treat it as a regression: diagnose which faults became untestable, for example through new tied logic, before promoting

D) Ignore coverage for scan insertion
problems.a: Treat it as a regression: diagnose which faults became untestable, for example through new tied logic, before promoting
problems.e: Equivalence proves function; it does not prove testability. A coverage drop is a golden-test failure.

problems.q:
An agent's DFT reward is chain count balance. What could go wrong?

A) It will reduce coverage to zero

B) Nothing: balance is always good

C) It may balance chains by crossing clock domains without lockup latches, creating hold failures in shift

D) It will remove scan entirely
problems.a: It may balance chains by crossing clock domains without lockup latches, creating hold failures in shift
problems.e: A proxy reward must be paired with the invariants (domain rules, timing) or the agent will trade them away.

problems.q:
An agent inserts scan and all checks pass, but test coverage dropped 0.5 points versus baseline. What is the right action?

A) Lower the baseline

B) Treat it as a regression: diagnose which faults became untestable, for example through new tied logic, before promoting

C) Promote it, since equivalence passed

D) Ignore coverage for scan insertion
problems.a: Treat it as a regression: diagnose which faults became untestable, for example through new tied logic, before promoting
problems.e: Equivalence proves function; it does not prove testability. A coverage drop is a golden-test failure.

label: Golden tests on coverage and pattern counts
lesson:
# Golden tests on coverage and pattern counts

When an agent changes an ATPG or DFT skill, the evidence that it helped and did not hurt is a golden suite: reference designs with known baseline coverage and pattern counts, and tolerances the new run must meet. Writing the checks precisely, per design and per metric, is what turns an agent's claim into something a reviewer can approve.

## Per-design limits

A golden test fixes, for each reference design, the baseline test coverage and pattern count, and a tolerance for each: for example, coverage may not drop by more than 0.05 percentage points and pattern count may not grow by more than 2 percent. A design fails if either limit is violated, and the change fails if any design fails. A design whose coverage moved from 97.81 to 97.68 percent fails on coverage even if its pattern count fell; one whose pattern count grew from 9073 to 9798 (8 percent) fails even though coverage barely moved. Gains on some designs never excuse a regression on another.

## Computing the thresholds

Ceilings are computed exactly so that the check is deterministic. With a baseline of 19,657 patterns and a 2 percent allowance, the largest passing count is $\lfloor 19{,}657 \times 1.02 \rfloor = 20{,}050$. Coverage is recomputed from raw counts rather than taken from a rounded report: with $T$ faults, $D$ detected and $U$ proven untestable, $TC = D/(T - U)$. Comparing to three decimals avoids flapping on rounding. Runs must be seeded and deterministic, or the suite will fail and pass at random.

## What the metric can hide

Golden metrics can be gamed. Test coverage rises when more faults are proven untestable even if fewer are detected: baseline 55,714 detected of 58,707 with 1761 untestable gives 97.84 percent; a run with 55,599 detected and 1941 untestable gives 97.94 percent, an apparent gain from detecting 115 fewer faults. A robust suite therefore checks detected counts and fault-list identity alongside coverage, verifies new untestable proofs, and adds a differential check that patterns for unchanged fault classes still detect the same faults.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum (golden and differential testing, tool-grounded rewards).

problems.q: An agent changed the ATPG skill's fault-ordering policy. The golden suite fails a design if test coverage drops by more than 0.05 percentage points or the pattern count grows by more than 3 percent. Results: D1: baseline 96.72 percent with 5347 patterns, new 96.71 percent with 5625 patterns; D2: baseline 99.33 percent with 7410 patterns, new 99.36 percent with 7432 patterns; D3: baseline 97.68 percent with 9856 patterns, new 97.62 percent with 10181 patterns; D4: baseline 97.32 percent with 18210 patterns, new 97.28 percent with 18993 patterns; D5: baseline 98.38 percent with 16009 patterns, new 98.28 percent with 16617 patterns. How many designs fail?
problems.e: Failing: D1, D3, D4, D5. Both limits are checked per design; a gain on one design does not excuse a regression on another.

How many designs fail?
problems.e: Failing: D1, D2, D3, D4, D5, D6. Both limits are checked per design; a gain on one design does not excuse a regression on another.

The golden suite fails a design if test coverage drops by more than 0.02 percentage points or the pattern count grows by more than 2 percent. Results: D1: baseline 95.01 percent with 2709 patterns, new 95.09 percent with 2895 patterns; D2: baseline 97.47 percent with 10274 patterns, new 97.53 percent with 10325 patterns; D3: baseline 98.97 percent with 13244 patterns, new 98.92 percent with 13111 patterns; D4: baseline 98.34 percent with 2678 patterns, new 98.39 percent with 2651 patterns; D5: baseline 96.28 percent with 9823 patterns, new 96.31 percent with 10500 patterns; D6: baseline 95.08 percent with 16553 patterns, new 94.97 percent with 16751 patterns; D7: baseline 95.45 percent with 6834 patterns, new 95.39 percent with 6560 patterns. label: Diagnosis agents that read failure logs
lesson:
# Diagnosis agents that read failure logs

Volume diagnosis produces thousands of candidate lists, and someone must decide which dies go to physical failure analysis, a slow and destructive lab step. A diagnosis agent reads tester failure logs, calls the diagnosis engine as a tool, combines its scores with layout and defect statistics, and proposes a ranked list, with a human approving what is sent to the lab. The quantitative core is Bayesian ranking.

## Posterior ranking

Each candidate defect has a **prior** from layout and process statistics: critical area, layer defect densities, history of similar failures. The diagnosis engine supplies a **likelihood**: how well the candidate explains the observed failures. The posterior is proportional to prior times likelihood, normalized over candidates:
$$P(c_i \mid \text{log}) = \frac{\pi_i \, \ell_i}{\sum_j \pi_j \, \ell_j}.$$
With prior weights 4, 1, 2, 2 and likelihoods 0.34, 0.27, 0.29, 0.89, the products are 1.36, 0.27, 0.58, 1.78, and the top candidate's posterior is $1.78/3.99 = 44.6$ percent. A candidate with the best match score need not be most probable if its prior is low.

## Choosing what to send

Failure analysis costs a day or more per candidate, so the agent sends candidates in order of posterior until their total reaches a confidence target. With posteriors 45, 25.1, 20.3 and 9.6 percent, reaching 80 percent takes three candidates. A good agent reports this reasoning and the cost explicitly, and stops early when posteriors are flat, which signals that the diagnosis is ambiguous and more patterns (diagnostic ATPG) would be cheaper than lab time.

## Likelihoods from mismatches

A simple likelihood model counts mismatches $m$ between a candidate's predicted and observed failing patterns and sets $\ell = \epsilon^m$ for a small error rate $\epsilon$, for example 0.1. Each mismatch then costs a factor of 10, and a perfect match beats a single-mismatch candidate unless its prior is more than ten times smaller. Agents must treat logs as data, not instructions, keep the design and logs inside the IP boundary, and have their rankings scored against later failure-analysis results, which is the ground truth for improving the model.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum (agentic loops, tool-grounded evaluation); Wang, Wu and Wen (2006), chapter 7 on diagnosis.

label: Fast fault-sampled coverage in an agent loop
prereqs: Fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop
lesson:
# Fast fault-sampled coverage in an agent loop

An agent exploring DFT configurations cannot afford full fault simulation of millions of faults for every candidate. A fast mode simulates a uniform random sample of faults and reports the sample coverage with a confidence interval. Knowing the interval tells the agent when the fast answer is good enough and when it must recurse to the accurate engine.

## Sampled coverage

If $n$ faults are drawn uniformly from the full list and $d$ are detected, $\hat{p} = d/n$ is an unbiased estimate of the full coverage. Its cost is proportional to $n$, not to the full fault count: sampling 10,000 of 2 million faults is 200 times cheaper. With 9864 of 10,000 detected, the fast mode reports 98.64 percent. Sampling must be uniform over the same fault list (collapsed or not) that the full coverage uses, or the estimate is biased.

## Confidence

By the central limit theorem, $\hat{p}$ is approximately normal with standard deviation $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$, so the 95 percent confidence half-width is
$$h = 1.96\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}.$$
At $\hat{p} = 0.9$ and $n = 1000$, $h = 1.86$ percentage points; at $n = 10{,}000$ and $\hat{p} = 0.986$, about 0.23 points. Coverage near 100 percent has small variance, which helps, but sign-off decisions are often about differences of a few hundredths of a point.

## When to recurse

To reach half-width $h$, the sample size must be
$$n = \left\lceil \frac{1.96^2 \, p(1-p)}{h^2} \right\rceil.$$
At $p = 0.942$ and $h = 0.05$ points (0.0005), that is about 840,000 faults, approaching the full list. So the agent uses sampling to discard clearly worse configurations, and recurses to full fault simulation when two candidates differ by less than about twice the half-width, or when the result feeds sign-off. Sampled estimates are also a reward-hacking risk if an agent can choose the sample, so the harness, not the agent, draws the seed.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum (fast and accurate engines); standard texts on survey sampling for the binomial confidence interval.
